All sums are finite, so these curves are smooth. Every coordinate of
$y(t)$ remains strictly between zero and one, since both coordinate
values occur among the positive-probability face atoms.

Define the covariance matrix
\[
 K=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_x}p_a(a-x)(a-x)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Differentiation gives $p_a'(0)=p_a v\cdot(a-x)$ and $y'(0)=Kv$.
For every $w$, we have
$w^{\mathsf T}Kw=\sum_a p_a(w\cdot(a-x))^2$.
Positivity of $p$ and the spanning of $T$ by $a-x$ therefore give
\begin{equation}\label{ent:covariance-range}
                 \ker K=T^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{im}K=T,
                 \qquad \rank K=d.
\end{equation}
Also $y''(0)\in T$, since the curve stays in $x+T$.

Let $g=\nabla J_c(x)$ and let $D$ be its diagonal Hessian:
\[
 g_e=-\log x_e-c\log(1-x_e)-(c+1),\qquad
 D_{ee}=-\frac1{x_e}+\frac{c}{1-x_e}.
\]
Since $\Phi'(t)=v\cdot y(t)$, Equation~\eqref{ent:tilt-entropy}
gives $\frac{d}{dt}H(y(t))=-(\theta+tv)\cdot y'(t)$.
For $r(t)=J_c(y(t))-H(y(t))$, the first two derivatives at zero are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 r'(0)&=(g+\theta)\cdot Kv,\\
 r''(0)&=(Kv)^{\mathsf T}D(Kv)+v^{\mathsf T}Kv
                       +(g+\theta)\cdot y''(0).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Stationarity gives $r'(0)=0$ for every $v$. Since $\operatorname{im}K=T$
and $y''(0)\in T$, the last term in $r''(0)$ vanishes. The second
derivative test is therefore
\begin{equation}\label{ent:second-variation}
 0\ge (Kv)^{\mathsf T}D(Kv)+v^{\mathsf T}Kv
 \qquad(v\in\R^E).
\end{equation}
This cancellation is why differentiating within the minimal face suffices;
no smoothness of $H$ across different faces has been assumed.

Take orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1,\ldots,u_d$ of $K$ with positive
eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$. Substituting $v=u_i$ in
Equation~\eqref{ent:second-variation}, dividing by $\lambda_i$, and
summing gives
\[
             0\ge d+\sum_i\lambda_i u_i^{\mathsf T}Du_i
                    =d+\tr(KD).
\]
Only the spectral decomposition of $K$ is used; $K$ and $D$ need not
commute. If $d=0$, this same statement is the empty sum identity.
Each coordinate is Boolean, so $K_{ee}=x_e(1-x_e)$. Using
$\sum_e x_e=m$, we obtain
\[
 \tr(KD)=\sum_e\bigl[-(1-x_e)+cx_e\bigr]=-s+(c+1)m,
\]
which proves Equation~\eqref{ent:trace-obstruction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Lower bound in Theorem~\ref{ent:main}]
Write the original vertex count as $2M\ge2$, and fix
$c=2-2/M+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$.
By Lemma~\ref{ent:continuity}, $J_c-H$ attains a maximum on $P(G)$.
Suppose that this maximum is positive, at $x$. Delete its zero edges
and the endpoints of its value-one edges. The exact fractional reduction
in Lemma~\ref{geom:lem-reduction} identifies all laws of mean $x$ with laws
of the reduced mean and preserves $F,B,H$. An empty reduction would give
$F=B=H=0$, contrary to positivity. The reduced graph therefore has
$2m$ vertices for some $1\le m\le M$, and all retained coordinates are
strictly fractional.

Every feasible mean in the reduced graph extends by the fixed matching
edges to a feasible original mean, preserving the same three functions.
The reduced mean consequently remains a global maximum of $J_c-H$.
The geometric rank bound gives $d\ge s-3m+2$, whereas
Lemma~\ref{ent:trace} gives
\[
 0\ge d-s+(c+1)m\ge 2+(c-2)m
       =2\left(1-\frac mM\right)+\varepsilon m>0.
\]
This contradiction proves $H\ge F-cB$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
For each fixed mean, $B$ is finite; letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$
proves $H\ge F-(2-2/M)B$. The strict coefficient followed by this limit
is essential: the displayed geometric comparison can be an equality
when $m=M$ and $\varepsilon=0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The upper bound and componentwise refinement}

The upper bound is the vertex-star instance of Shearer's entropy
inequality~\citep[Section~V, inequality~(22)]{ChungGrahamFranklShearer1986}.
We give the short chain-rule proof to make the counting of parallel
edge coordinates explicit.

\begin{proof}[Upper bound in Theorem~\ref{ent:main}]
Let $X=(X_e)_{e\in E}$ be the incidence vector of any matching law with
mean $x$, and order $E$. For a vertex $v$, the chain rule gives
\[
 \Ent(X_{\delta(v)})
 =\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}
   \Ent\bigl(X_e\mid X_f:f\in\delta(v),\ f<e\bigr)
 \ge\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}\Ent\bigl(X_e\mid X_f:f<e\bigr).
\]
Conditioning on additional finite random variables decreases conditional
entropy, by concavity of entropy applied to the conditional laws.
Every edge, including every labelled parallel edge, belongs to exactly
two vertex stars. Summing and applying the chain rule again therefore gives
$\sum_v\Ent(X_{\delta(v)})\ge2\Ent(X)$.
At a vertex the star vector makes exactly one choice, with probabilities
$(x_e)_{e\in\delta(v)}$, so
\[
 \Ent(X)\le\frac12\sum_v\left[-\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\log x_e\right]
 =F(x).
\]
Taking the maximum over laws proves the upper bound, including fixed
coordinates and disconnected graphs.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Fractional components]\label{ent:components}
For $x\in P(G)$, remove its zero edges and the endpoints of its value-one
edges. Let the nonempty connected components of the remaining graph have
$2m_i$ vertices, and let $B_i$ denote the sum defining $B$ on component $i$.
Then
\[
                 F(x)-\sum_i(2-2/m_i)B_i(x)\le H(x)\le F(x).
\]
If there are no remaining components, $F(x)=B(x)=H(x)=0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The exact reduction preserves the functions. Every residual component
has a perfect matching, hence even positive order. A law of a whole
matching induces matching laws on the components, whose entropies sum
to at least the joint entropy. Conversely, the independent product of
component maximizing laws realizes the prescribed mean and the sum of
their entropies. Thus $H$, like $F$ and $B$, is additive at these fixed
component means. Apply Theorem~\ref{ent:main} separately to each component.
\end{proof}

\section{Entropy and counting consequences}
\label{cons:section}

The pointwise entropy bound has two kinds of counting consequences.
Maximizing a separable entropy objective estimates the total matching
count, while evaluating it at a feasible uniform mean gives lower counts
from structural hypotheses. Throughout this section, unless
an empty graph is explicitly mentioned, \(G\) is a finite loopless
multigraph on \(2m>0\) vertices with at least one perfect matching.
Parallel edges retain their individual labels. Write \(P=P(G)\),
\(N=|\mathcal M(G)|\), and recall that \(F\), \(B\), and \(H\) use
natural logarithms. For every \(x\in P\), Theorem~\ref{ent:main} gives
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:input}
 F(x)-\left(2-\frac2m\right)B(x)\le H(x)\le F(x).
\end{equation}
The elementary scalar estimate
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:complement}
 0\le -(1-u)\ln(1-u)\le u\qquad(0\le u\le1)
\end{equation}
will be used repeatedly. Indeed,
\(u+(1-u)\ln(1-u)\) vanishes at zero and has derivative
\(-\ln(1-u)\ge0\) on \([0,1)\); continuity gives the endpoint.
Every perfect matching has \(m\) edges, so \(\sum_e x_e=m\) and
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:B-bound}
                         0\le B(x)\le m.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Entropy defects and separable counting estimates}

\begin{corollary}[Entropy-dependent defect]
\label{cons:defect}
For every \(x\in P\),
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:defect-bound}
 0\le F(x)-H(x)
 \le \min\{F(x),\,2m-2\}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The first inequality follows from \(H\le F\). Nonnegativity of
entropy gives \(F-H\le F\), while
Equations~\eqref{cons:input} and~\eqref{cons:B-bound} give
\(F-H\le(2-2/m)B\le2m-2\).
This includes \(m=1\), when the defect is zero.
\end{proof}

Define the binary-coordinate entropy by
\[
 H_{\mathrm{bin}}(x)
   =\sum_e[-x_e\ln x_e-(1-x_e)\ln(1-x_e)]
   =F(x)+B(x).
\]
The word ``binary'' refers to an edge indicator's two values;
these entropies are still measured with natural logarithms.

\begin{corollary}[Separable estimates of the matching count]
\label{cons:entropy-count}
One has
\begin{align}
 \ln N&\le\max_{x\in P}F(x)\le\ln N+2m-2,
       \label{cons:F-count}\\
 \ln N&\le\max_{x\in P}H_{\mathrm{bin}}(x)
                         \le\ln N+3m-2.
       \label{cons:binary-count}
\end{align}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The entropy comparison in Equation~\eqref{ent:comparison}, applied to
the uniform law, gives entropy at most \(\ln N\) for every law on
\(N\) outcomes, with equality for the uniform law.
At the mean \(\bar x\) of the uniform matching law we therefore have
\(H(\bar x)=\ln N\). Equation~\eqref{cons:input} gives
\(\ln N\le F(\bar x)\le H_{\mathrm{bin}}(\bar x)\), proving both
lower estimates. Corollary~\ref{cons:defect} gives
\(F(x)\le H(x)+2m-2\le\ln N+2m-2\) at every \(x\in P\).
Also,
\[
 H_{\mathrm{bin}}(x)-H(x)
 \le\left(3-\frac2m\right)B(x)\le3m-2.
\]
Taking maxima proves the upper estimates. The maxima exist because
\(P\) is compact and both separable functions are continuous.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Uniform marginals and structural lower counts}

\begin{theorem}[Many edge-disjoint perfect matchings]
\label{cons:structural}
Let \(G\) be a finite loopless multigraph on \(2m>0\) vertices that
contains \(k\ge1\) pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings.
If \(k=1\), then \(N(G)\ge1\). If \(k\ge2\), then
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:finite-order-count}
 N(G)\ge k^m(1-1/k)^{2(m-1)(k-1)}
       \ge e^{-2(m-1)}k^m
       \ge(e^{-2}k)^m.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \(M_1,\ldots,M_k\) be the selected matchings and take their
uniform mixture. Its mean
\[
                 x=\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^k\mathbf1_{M_i}\in P(G)
\]
is \(1/k\) on their union of \(km\) labeled edges and zero on every
other edge. In particular, the hypotheses do not require all ambient
edges to belong to that union. We have \(F(x)=m\ln k\).
If \(k=1\), the selected matching already gives \(N(G)\ge1\).
For \(k\ge2\), direct evaluation yields
\[
                 B(x)=-m(k-1)\ln(1-1/k).
\]
Since \(H(x)\le\ln N(G)\), Theorem~\ref{ent:main} now gives
\[
 \ln N(G)\ge m\ln k+2(m-1)(k-1)\ln(1-1/k).
\]
Exponentiating proves the first inequality in
Equation~\eqref{cons:finite-order-count}.
The function \(\ln(1-u)+u/(1-u)\) starts at zero and has derivative
\(u/(1-u)^2\ge0\) for \(0\le u<1\). Thus
\((k-1)\ln(1-1/k)\ge-1\), giving the second inequality; the third
uses \(m-1\le m\).
\end{proof}

At \(m=1\), the finite-order estimate is simply
\(N(G)\ge k\), the exact count on the selected parallel-edge subgraph.
We keep \(k=1\) separate to avoid an undefined power at zero.

Only feasibility of the uniform mean enters the preceding proof. It
therefore applies to the following class without requiring a partition
of its edges into perfect matchings.

\begin{corollary}[Regular graphs with large odd cuts]
\label{cons:regular}
Let \(G\) be a finite loopless \(k\)-regular multigraph on \(2m>0\)
vertices, where \(k\ge1\). Suppose
\(\lvert\delta(S)\rvert\ge k\) for every odd vertex set \(S\).
Then the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{cons:structural} hold.
In particular, they hold for every \((k-1)\)-edge-connected
\(k\)-regular graph of positive even order.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The vector \(x_e=1/k\) has unit degree sums, and the cut hypothesis
gives \(x(\delta(S))\ge1\) for every odd \(S\).
Theorem~\ref{geom:thm-polytope} implies \(x\in P(G)\); in particular,
\(G\) has a perfect matching. Since \(|E|=km\), the evaluations of
\(F(x)\) and \(B(x)\) in the preceding proof apply unchanged when
\(k\ge2\). For \(k=1\), the graph itself is a perfect matching.

For the final assertion, an odd \(S\) is nonempty and proper because
\(|V(G)|\) is even. Edge connectivity gives
\(\lvert\delta(S)\rvert\ge k-1\), while summing degrees in \(S\)
gives
\[
            k|S|=2|E(S)|+|\delta(S)|.
\]
Consequently \(|\delta(S)|\equiv k\pmod2\); it cannot equal \(k-1\)
and is therefore at least \(k\). Parallel edges are counted with
multiplicity in this identity.
\end{proof}

The odd-cut hypothesis is a condition on the uniform vector. Requiring
merely that every edge lie in some perfect matching does not assert
that condition. At small degree the exponential base in
Equation~\eqref{cons:finite-order-count} can be below one, so these
estimates do not supply the classical cubic exponential lower bound.

The empty graph has one empty perfect matching. Its count is handled
directly, without using expressions that divide by \(m\); for
\(k\ge1\), the homogeneous coarse bound \((e^{-2}k)^m\)
is interpreted as one.
When \(k=0\) and the vertex set is nonempty, the coarse
bound is zero, while formulas containing \(1/k\) are not asserted.
In particular, specifying no selected matchings places no restriction
on the ambient edge set.

The weaker separable and nonlinear comparisons and their structural
consequences appear with the alternative proofs in Appendix~\ref{a:section}.
The next section examines sharp face codimension and the obstruction to
coefficient one. Section~\ref{cons:weighted-section} then passes from
these entropy estimates to weighted partition functions.

\section{Weighted partition functions}\label{cons:weighted-section}
\label{d:sec-weighted-interface}

Let $G$ be a loopless labelled multigraph on $n=2m\ge2$ vertices with
at least one perfect matching. Write $P=P(G)$. We pass from natural-log
entropy to binary-log weights, so that the resulting estimate can be
used by the rational counting algorithm.

Put
\[
 h_2(x)=\frac{F(x)}{\ln2}=\sum_{e\in E}-x_e\log_2x_e,
 \qquad 0\log_2 0=0.
\]
For \(\beta\in\mathbb R^E\), define
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:weighted-definitions}
 Z_\beta=\sum_{M\in\mathcal M(G)}2^{\beta\cdot\mathbf1_M},
 \qquad
 q^*=\max_{x\in P}
        [h_2(x)+\beta\cdot x].
\end{equation}
The maximum exists by continuity on the compact matching polytope.

\begin{corollary}[Weighted counting estimate]
\label{cons:weighted}
For every finite real vector \(\beta\),
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:weighted-bracket}
                q^*-\frac{2m-2}{\ln2}
                \le\log_2 Z_\beta\le q^*.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let \(p_\beta(M)=2^{\beta\cdot\mathbf1_M}/Z_\beta\), a positive
probability law on the matching family. The finite entropy comparison
with this law gives, for any matching law \(p\) of mean \(x\),
\[
 \frac{-\sum_Mp(M)\ln p(M)}{\ln2}+\beta\cdot x
                          \le\log_2 Z_\beta,
\]
with equality for \(p=p_\beta\). Indeed, this is the nonnegativity
of \(\sum_{M:p(M)>0}p(M)\ln(p(M)/p_\beta(M))\), which follows
from \(\ln t\le t-1\).
Taking a maximizing law at each mean and then the maximum over means
therefore yields
\begin{equation}
 \label{cons:variational}
 \log_2 Z_\beta
       =\max_{x\in P}\left[\frac{H(x)}{\ln2}+\beta\cdot x\right].
\end{equation}
Corollary~\ref{cons:defect} says
\(F(x)-(2m-2)\le H(x)\le F(x)\).
Divide by \(\ln2\), add \(\beta\cdot x\), and maximize to obtain
Equation~\eqref{cons:weighted-bracket}.
\end{proof}

The analytical comparison does not itself supply a numerical optimizer.
The exact-arithmetic construction in
Sections~\ref{d:sec-objective}--\ref{d:sec-algorithm} uses the following
coarser bracket, with fixed constants that leave room for its later
rounding and optimization errors.

\begin{corollary}[Conservative weighted bracket]
\label{d:coarse-weighted}
For every finite loopless labelled multigraph on an even number
\(n\ge2\) of vertices with at least one perfect matching, and every
finite real vector \(\beta\in\mathbb R^E\),
\begin{equation}
 \label{d:eq-coarse-weighted}
 q^*-4n\le\log_2 Z_\beta\le q^*+n.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
With \(n=2m\), Corollary~\ref{cons:weighted} gives
\[
 q^*-\frac{n-2}{\ln2}\le\log_2Z_\beta\le q^*.
\]
Since \(\ln2=\int_1^2t^{-1}\,dt\ge1/2\), we have
\((n-2)/\ln2\le2n-4\le4n\). Enlarging both sides of this bracket
proves the claim.
\end{proof}

For the empty graph, the matching family consists of the
empty matching, \(Z_\beta=1\) and \(q^*=0\). The counting algorithm
handles that input directly. On positive even order it uses exactly
Equation~\eqref{d:eq-coarse-weighted}; all constants in the finite
optimization and final estimate below refer to this bracket.

\section{Triangle expansions and sharp face codimension}
\label{ex:sec-triangle-expansions}

Extremal rank examples already occur among the cubic staircases of
Abdi et al.~\cite[discussion after Corollary~6.6 and Figure~2]{AbdiCornuejolsDadushDalirrooyfard2026}.
They have exactly three perfect matchings meeting every minimum odd
cut once, and those cut rows have rank \(|E|-2\).
We give an explicit triangle-expansion construction and derive the
associated prescribed-marginal entropy formulas. This also gives
a necessary lower bound on a universal entropy coefficient.
The construction underlying Klee graphs is standard;
see Cygan, Pilipczuk, and \v{S}krekovski
\citep[Section~1 and Lemma~2.1]{CyganPilipczukSkrekovski2013}
on the triangle expansions and the unique partition into three perfect
matchings, up to permutation. We give the construction and the argument
needed here. Balanced matching laws on cubic graphs and triangle
contractions also occur in the corrected full version of

\subsection{Expansion and contraction}

and adding \(f_i\). Conversely, contracting \(T\) in a perfect
matching of \(G'\) that crosses \(\delta(T)\) once recovers

\subsection{A triangular minimal face for every order}

Begin with two vertices joined by three distinct labelled parallel
edges. Its three one-edge perfect matchings partition its edge set.
Repeatedly expand any vertex as above. Each expansion adds two
vertices and three edges, and all degrees remain three. Denote
any graph obtained after \(m-1\) expansions by \(G_m\), so that
\[
 |V(G_m)|=2m,\qquad |E(G_m)|=3m.
\]
The three initial perfect matchings extend uniquely at each step.
Their extensions \(M_1,M_2,M_3\) still partition the edge set:
the old edges retain their partition, and \(f_i\) belongs to the
extension of the matching containing \(e_i\). In particular,
\[
 x^{(m)}=\tfrac13\bigl(a(M_1)+a(M_2)+a(M_3)\bigr)
\]
has every coordinate equal to \(1/3\) and belongs to the full
perfect-matching polytope.

The first expansion gives \(K_4\); subsequent expansions preserve
simplicity. Thus \(G_m\) is simple for every \(m\ge2\), and these
are Klee graphs. Only the starting case \(m=1\) needs parallel
edges.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp codimension and prescribed-marginal entropy]
\label{ex:prop-klee-face}
For every integer \(m\ge1\), the graph \(G_m\) and the point
\(x^{(m)}\) above satisfy
\[
 F_{x^{(m)}}=
 \operatorname{conv}\{a(M_1),a(M_2),a(M_3)\},
 \qquad d(x^{(m)})=2.
\]
The unique law on perfect matchings with mean \(x^{(m)}\) is the
uniform law on \(M_1,M_2,M_3\). Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{ex:eq-klee-values}
 \begin{aligned}
 |E(G_m)|-d(x^{(m)})&=3m-2,\\
 H(x^{(m)})&=\ln3,\\
 F(x^{(m)})&=m\ln3,\\
 B(x^{(m)})&=2m\ln(3/2).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For \(m=1\), the three matching vectors are the three coordinate
vectors in \(\mathbb R^3\), and \(P(G_1)\) is their simplex.
Its uniform point is in its relative interior. Repeated application
of Lemma~\ref{ex:lem-expansion-face} shows that the minimal face at
\(x^{(m)}\) is the image of this simplex, with vertices
\(a(M_1),a(M_2),a(M_3)\). In particular its dimension is two.

One can also see the restriction on laws directly. For the last
inserted triangle, a law with edge marginals \(1/3\) has expected
cut-crossing count \(3(1/3)=1\). Since each matching crosses this
cut once or three times, it must cross once almost surely.
Contraction gives a law on the preceding graph with the same
uniform marginals, and the crossing-one extension is unique.
Iterating leaves only the three initial matchings. Thus the
original law is supported on \(M_1,M_2,M_3\). Since these
matchings partition the edges, the marginal of any edge in
\(M_i\) equals the probability assigned to \(M_i\), which must
be \(1/3\). This proves uniqueness and the entropy formula.

There are \(3m\) edges, all with marginal \(1/3\). Substitution
in the definitions of \(F\) and \(B\) gives the remaining
formulas.
\end{proof}

All coordinates here are strictly between zero and one.
Equation~\eqref{ex:eq-klee-values} therefore attains the bound in
Proposition~\ref{geom:prop-rank} for every \(m\ge1\). Equivalently,
by Equation~\eqref{geom:eq-rank}, the tight odd-cut rows have rank
\(3m-2\). The dimension two is the dimension of the minimal face
at \(x^{(m)}\); the whole perfect-matching polytope can have
additional vertices.

\begin{corollary}[Restriction on a universal entropy coefficient]
\label{ex:cor-coefficient}
If a constant \(c\) satisfies
\[
 H(x)\ge F(x)-cB(x)
\]
for every finite loopless multigraph \(G\) and every
\(x\in P(G)\), then
\[
 c\ge\frac{\ln3}{2\ln(3/2)}.
\]
The same necessary bound holds if the assertion is restricted to
simple graphs.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Applying the asserted inequality to \(G_m,x^{(m)}\) gives
\[
 c\ge
 \frac{(m-1)\ln3}{2m\ln(3/2)}.
\]
Let \(m\) tend to infinity. The graphs with \(m\ge2\) are simple,
so the same limit applies under that restriction.
\end{proof}

The necessary coefficient in Corollary~\ref{ex:cor-coefficient} lies
strictly between $1$ and the universal coefficient $2$ supplied by
Theorem~\ref{ent:main}. Sharpness of the geometric estimate therefore
does not settle the optimal entropy coefficient. The next example makes
the failure of coefficient one explicit at a fixed order.

\subsection{An eight-vertex obstruction to coefficient one}

For a concrete instance, take vertex set \(\{0,1,\ldots,7\}\) and
edge set
\[
 E=\{01,03,05,14,16,23,24,27,34,56,57,67\},
\]
where \(ij\) denotes the undirected edge with endpoints \(i,j\).
Contracting the triangles \(T=\{2,3,4\}\) and
\(U=\{5,6,7\}\) gives \(K_4\). Thus this graph is obtained by
expanding two vertices of \(K_4\), and is an instance of \(G_4\).

Its five perfect matchings are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 M_1&=\{01,27,34,56\},&
 M_2&=\{03,16,24,57\},\\
 M_3&=\{05,14,23,67\},&
 N_1&=\{03,14,27,56\},\\
 &&N_2&=\{05,16,27,34\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
This list follows without enumeration software. A matching uses
one of \(01,03,05\). If it uses \(01\), the remaining two odd
triangles are joined only by \(27\), forcing \(M_1\). If it uses
\(03\), vertex \(1\) is matched by \(14\) or \(16\), after which
the remaining edges are forced, giving \(N_1\) or \(M_2\).
If it uses \(05\), the same two choices at vertex \(1\) force
\(M_3\) or \(N_2\).

The cuts
\[
 \delta(T)=\{03,14,27\},\qquad
 \delta(U)=\{05,16,27\}
\]
both have total marginal one at \(x_e=1/3\).
The matching \(N_1\) crosses the first cut three times, and
\(N_2\) crosses the second cut three times. They therefore have
probability zero in every law with those marginals. The remaining
three matchings partition \(E\), so their probabilities are all
\(1/3\). In particular the relevant entropy is \(\ln3\), even
though the graph has five perfect matchings in total.

At this feasible point of the full polytope,
\[
 H(x)=\ln3,\qquad
 F(x)-B(x)=4\ln(4/3)>\ln3,
\]
because \( (4/3)^4=256/81>3\).
The difference \(F(x)-B(x)-H(x)\) is
\(\ln(256/243)>0\). This gives a simple eight-vertex
counterexample to the coefficient-one lower bound.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph. A perfect matching is a
set of edges incident to each vertex exactly once. Write
\[
 Z(G)=\#\{M\subseteq E:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }G\}.
\]
A fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme approximates $Z(G)$
within a prescribed relative error, with a prescribed success probability,
in time polynomial in the input length and the reciprocal error.
The confidence parameter enters through its logarithm. We prove the
following theorem, including a bound on the time of every execution.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
There is a uniform classical randomized algorithm which, given $G$ and
rational parameters $0<\eps<1$ and $0<\delta<1/2$, returns a nonnegative
rational number $\widehat Z$ such that
\[
 \Prb\bigl[(1-\eps)Z(G)\le \widehat Z\le(1+\eps)Z(G)\bigr]
 \ge 1-\delta.
\]
If $Z(G)=0$, the output is zero with certainty. The worst-case bit running
time is polynomial in the input encoding length, $\eps^{-1}$, and
$\log\delta^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

edge subsets with prescribed vertex degrees and for matchings of a
specified size. On feasible inputs, its samplers always return a
feasible object and approximate the corresponding uniform law in total

# I25 resumed — A rooted entropy budget closes the coefficient-3/2 induction

Date: 2026-10-09. Corpus premise: all supplied proofs at `openai/math@fd4aeeb2ee4fc729c18d98444fed42fd0529eeeb` are accepted as true.

**Disposition: complete candidate proof, ready for separate independent proof and significance review.** For every finite loopless labelled multigraph with a perfect matching, the requested prescribed-mean coefficient $3/2$ follows from the stronger rooted inequality proved below. The additional bridge is a vertex-star reserve that pays every tight-cut separator exactly. It allows induction to remove nontrivial tight cuts *before* applying the covariance trace, replacing the general supported-face codimension bound by the degree-equation bound. Neither the new proof nor its significance has independent acceptance. No priority claim or accepted-count change is requested.

The original I25 was cancelled before a report/seal; the cause is unestablished. Its partial artifacts and commentary are not premises. The original and resumed task JSON, AGENTS.md, full I22 report, current ledger and complete preprint tree are frozen in [inputs.json](../sources/i25_matching_entropy_improvement_resumed/inputs.json). The original source/experiment trees, including vendor files, were read only: [original-checkpoint.json](../sources/i25_matching_entropy_improvement_resumed/original-checkpoint.json) records all 1,226 files. Only the assigned resumed report/source/experiment paths were written. No agents, index edits, staging, commits, pushes, or other-project edits were made.

## 1. Exact candidate and scope

Let $G=(V,E)$ be any finite undirected loopless multigraph, with parallel edges distinguished by labels, $|V|=2m\ge2$, and at least one perfect matching. Write $P(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_M:M\text{ perfect}\}$. For **every** $x\in P(G)$, including boundary means, use natural logarithms and $0\log0=0$, and define

\[
 H_G(x)=\max_{\mathbb E\mathbf1_M=x}\operatorname{Ent}(M),\quad
 F_G(x)=-\sum_e x_e\log x_e,\quad
 B_G(x)=-\sum_e(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e),\quad D_G=F_G-H_G.
\]

For a vertex $v$, put

\[
 b_v(x)=-\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e),\qquad
 W_{G,v}(x)=B_G(x)-b_v(x)
           =-\sum_{e\notin\delta(v)}(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e).
\]

**Rooted theorem (candidate).** For every such $G,x$, and **every** $v\in V$,

\[
 \boxed{\quad D_G(x)\le\frac32 W_{G,v}(x).\quad}                 \tag{R}
\]

In particular,

\[
 H_G(x)\ge F_G(x)-\frac32\bigl(B_G(x)-\max_v b_v(x)\bigr)
          \ge F_G(x)-\frac32(1-1/m)B_G(x)
          \ge F_G(x)-\frac32 B_G(x).                         \tag{U}
\]

The middle step uses $\sum_v b_v=2B$, hence $\max_v b_v\ge B/m$. No bound on degree, connectivity, edge multiplicity, or the number of tight cuts is imposed. Empty graphs have $F=B=H=0$ separately; (R) has no root on an empty graph. Graphs without perfect matchings have no feasible mean to which the assertion applies.

This is an entropy-existence theorem. The separator step gives an explicit conditional gluing rule **given** child laws. No polynomial prescribed-mean sampler or numerical optimizer is asserted. The proof of the universal leaf bound uses compactness and a second-variation contradiction.

## 2. Exact source interfaces and comparison with I22

The pinned source is *Entropy and Face Dimension of the Perfect-Matching Polytope*. Selected original bytes are independently checked against their Git blob hashes and the frozen complete tree; [pinned-manifest.json](../sources/i25_matching_entropy_improvement_resumed/pinned-manifest.json) records immutable raw URLs and SHA-256. [source-contracts.json](../sources/i25_matching_entropy_improvement_resumed/source-contracts.json) stores exact statement slices, and [read-passages.json](../sources/i25_matching_entropy_improvement_resumed/read-passages.json) identifies the proof passages used.

## 3. Tight-cut gluing and exact separator compensation

Let $S\subsetneq V$ be odd, with both sides of size at least three, $C=\delta(S)$, and $x(C)=1$. Orient the sides so that the designated root $v\in S$. Let $G_1$ retain $S$ and contract $V\setminus S$, and $G_2$ retain $V\setminus S$ and contract $S$ to $z$. Delete edges internal to the contracted side and retain every crossing edge label in each child. Edges becoming parallel remain distinct. Restrict $x$ to obtain feasible $x_1,x_2$; put $q=(x_e:e\in C)$, $h(q)=-\sum q_e\log q_e$, $b(q)=-\sum(1-q_e)\log(1-q_e)$.

Every matching with positive probability under a law of mean $x$ crosses $C$ once: its crossing count is odd and at least one, with expectation one. Such a parent matching is equivalent to two child matchings sharing their crossing label. If $L$ is this label, conditional subadditivity gives

\[
 \operatorname{Ent}(M_1,M_2)\le
 \operatorname{Ent}(M_1)+\operatorname{Ent}(M_2)-h(q).
\]

Conversely, take maximum-entropy child laws at their **fixed** means, draw $L\sim q$, and conditionally draw the children independently given $L$. Labels with $q_e=0$ are ignored. Source gluing produces a law of mean $x$, with equality in the display. Therefore

\[
 H_G=H_{G_1}+H_{G_2}-h(q),\quad
 F_G=F_{G_1}+F_{G_2}-h(q),\quad
 B_G=B_{G_1}+B_{G_2}-b(q).                               \tag{G}
\]

In particular $D_G=D_{G_1}+D_{G_2}$. The star of $v$ is unchanged in $G_1$, while the star of $z$ in $G_2$ is precisely $C$. Consequently

\[
 \boxed{W_{G,v}=W_{G_1,v}+W_{G_2,z}},\qquad
 \boxed{(D-cW)_{G,v}=(D-cW)_{G_1,v}+(D-cW)_{G_2,z}}.       \tag{A}
\]

One can also see the first identity edge by edge: crossing edges not incident to $v$ are charged exactly in $G_1$, and none are charged in $G_2$; every other charged edge occurs in just its retained side. Thus no entropy cancellation or independence assumption conceals the separator payment.

Iterate any finite sequence of nontrivial tight-cut splits, propagating the old root to the side retaining it and rooting the other side at its contracted vertex. The children strictly decrease in order. At every leaf $L$, let $r_L$ be its inherited root. Then

\[
 D_G=\sum_L D_L,\quad W_{G,v}=\sum_L W_{L,r_L},\quad
 \sum_L b_{r_L}=b_v+\sum_{\text{splits }C}b(q_C).             \tag{tree}
\]

The last identity follows by the same root propagation at each split. Applying (R) to the leaves leaves exactly enough reserve to pay **all** terms in (old), while retaining the original root reserve. Conditional gluing up the tree constructs the maximizing parent law from maximizing leaf laws. The matching of crossing marginals is fixed throughout; arbitrary independently chosen means would not suffice.

## 4. Base cases, parallel labels and boundary reductions

### 4.1 A self-contained ternary bound

For $p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)\in\Delta_3$, write $h=-\sum p_i\log p_i$, $b=-\sum(1-p_i)\log(1-p_i)$. We need only

\[
 h(p)\le\tfrac32 b(p).                                  \tag{T}
\]

Here is a complete scalar proof. Put $c=3/2$, $f(u)=-u\log u+c(1-u)\log(1-u)$. It has $f(0)=f(1)=0$, and $f''(u)=-1/u+c/(1-u)$, which changes from negative to positive at $a=1/(1+c)=2/5$. The continuous sum $\sum f(p_i)$ has a maximum. On the boundary it is $(1-c)h(p,1-p)\le0$. At an interior maximum all $f'(p_i)$ agree. Two coordinates above $a$, or one above and one equal to $a$, violate the second-derivative test in their difference direction. Two coordinates equal to $a$ contradict stationarity with the third, smaller coordinate, because $f'$ is strictly decreasing below $a$. If all are at most $a$, stationarity forces $p_i=1/3$, giving $\log3-3\log(3/2)=\log(8/9)<0$.

Otherwise one coordinate is above $a$, the other two are equal below $a$, and they have the form $t,t,1-2t$ with $0<t<1/3$. Set $g(t)=2f(t)+f(1-2t)$. With $u=(1-2t)/t\ge1$,

\[
 g'(t)/2=k(u)=\log u-c\log((u+1)/2),\qquad

\]

The function $k$ starts at zero at $u=1$, increases to a positive maximum, then decreases to minus infinity, with one further zero. As $t$ increases, $u$ decreases; hence $g$ first decreases and then increases. Its maximum is at an endpoint: $g(0)=0$, $g(1/3)=\log(8/9)<0$. This proves (T). I22's same elementary method gives the sharper $c_3=\log3/[2\log(3/2)]$; that sharp refinement is not needed for this proof.

### 4.2 Parallel-edge collapse preserves the entropy deficit

Collapse each parallel class $C_a$ to one edge of a simple graph and let $y_a=\sum_{e\in C_a}x_e\le1$. Write $r^a_e=x_e/y_a$ when $y_a>0$. A labelled matching consists of a collapsed matching and one label in every chosen class. For any law of mean $x$, the chain rule and conditional subadditivity bound its entropy by

\[
 H_{\rm simple}(y)+\sum_a y_a h(r^a).
\]

Indeed each selected-class label has aggregate conditional distribution $r^a$; conditioning additionally on the collapsed matching or other labels cannot increase its conditional entropy. Conversely choose a maximizing collapsed law and, given its matching, choose labels independently with these distributions. This realizes mean $x$ and equality. Also $F_G(x)=F_{\rm simple}(y)+\sum_a y_a h(r^a)$. Thus $D_G(x)=D_{\rm simple}(y)$.

For $\beta(u)=-(1-u)\log(1-u)$, concavity and $\beta(0)=0$ give $\sum_{e\in C_a}\beta(x_e)\ge\beta(y_a)$. Classes are either wholly incident or wholly nonincident to a given root, so $W_{G,v}(x)\ge W_{{\rm simple},v}(y)$. Therefore a rooted inequality for the collapsed graph implies it for the labelled multigraph. Zero classes contribute zero and require no conditional law.

### 4.3 Orders two and four

For two vertices every matching is a single label; $F=H$ and $W_v=0$.

On four vertices first use the preceding collapse. A simple graph has at most the three perfect matchings of $K_4$, which partition its six potential edges into pairs. A law is determined by their probabilities $p_1,p_2,p_3$, with zeroes for absent matching types; feasibility forces both edges of type $i$ to have mean $p_i$. Hence $H=h(p)$, $F=2h(p)$. At any root exactly one of each type's two edges is incident, so $W_v=b(p)$. Formula (T) proves (R), including subgraphs, missing types, and all boundary means. Collapse then gives the base case with any number of parallel labels.

### 4.4 Fixed coordinates in the induction

Deleting edges of mean zero changes none of $F,H,B,b_v,W_v$ and preserves the remaining matching laws at this mean. An edge of mean one belongs to every such law, exhausts the star at both endpoints, and all other incident coordinates are zero. Delete its endpoints and the forced edge, using the source's probability-preserving bijection. If the root survives, all its nonzero incident coordinates survive, so $W_v$ is unchanged. If the root is deleted, its original $b_v=0$, and $W_v=B$. On the residual smaller graph choose any root $w$; its rooted bound implies $D\le c(B-b_w)\le cB$ for $c\ge0$. If the residual graph is empty, $D=B=0$. Thus both root cases reduce to smaller order. Disconnected graphs need no special assumption or independent sampling assertion for this reduction.

## 5. Rooted covariance trace and the complete induction

For fixed root $v$ define $E_{c,v}=F-cW_v-H$. Suppose all retained coordinates satisfy $0<x_e<1$, and $E_{c,v}$ has a local maximum at $x$. Let $T$ be the minimal-face tangent space, $d=\dim T$, $s=|E|$. Take the source's positive maximizing exponential law on that face, with parameter $\theta$, covariance $K$, and tilt curve $y(t)$ for parameter $\theta+ta$. Then $y'(0)=Ka$, $y''(0)\in T$, $\operatorname{im}K=T$, and

\[
 H(y(t))=\log\sum_{M\text{ in face}}e^{(\theta+ta)\cdot\mathbf1_M}
              -(\theta+ta)\cdot y(t).
\]

Set $J=F-cW_v$. Its diagonal Hessian $A$ has

\[
 A_{ee}=-1/x_e+\frac{c\,\mathbf1_{e\notin\delta(v)}}{1-x_e}.
\]

Differentiation, exactly as in the source proof but retaining the indicator, gives

\[
 E'=(\nabla J+\theta)\cdot Ka=0,
\]

and then

\[
 0\ge E''=(Ka)^TA(Ka)+a^TKa+
                   (\nabla J+\theta)\cdot y''(0)
            =(Ka)^TA(Ka)+a^TKa.
\]

The last equality follows since the first-derivative equation for every $a$ makes $\nabla J+\theta\perp T$. Sum along positive eigenvectors of $K$, dividing each inequality by its positive eigenvalue. No commutation of $A,K$ is assumed. Because $K_{ee}=x_e(1-x_e)$, $\sum_e x_e=m$, and $\sum_{e\notin\delta(v)}x_e=m-1$, the necessary condition is

\[
 \boxed{0\ge d+\operatorname{tr}(KA)
             =d-s+m+c(m-1).}                            \tag{RT}
\]

**Induction proving (R).** Fix any $c=3/2+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon>0$. We prove $D\le cW_v$ simultaneously for every graph, feasible mean and root, by induction on $m$. Section 4 proves $m=1,2$. Suppose $m\ge3$, with the assertion known for every smaller order, and suppose a counterexample exists on a graph $G$ with root $v$. Compactness of $P(G)$ and continuity of $H,F,W_v$ give a **positive global maximum** of $E_{c,v}$, at $x$.

Delete zero edges. The retained point is still a global maximum on the resulting graph: every mean there zero-extends to the original graph with the same objective. If any value-one edge remains, Section 4.4 and induction contradict positivity. Thus all retained coordinates are strictly fractional.

If any nontrivial odd cut is tight at $x$, split it as in Section 3. Both child orders are smaller: if $|S|=2a-1$, then their orders are $2a$ and $2(m-a+1)$, with $2\le a\le m-1$. Only the $2m$ vertex-degree equations now constrain the minimal-face tangent space; coordinates are positive and every other odd-cut inequality is slack. Consequently $d\ge s-2m$. Applying (RT) yields

\[
 0\ge d-s+m+c(m-1)
   \ge(c-1)m-c
   =\frac{m-3}{2}+\varepsilon(m-1)>0.                   \tag{contradiction}
\]

This contradiction proves the induction for every $c>3/2$. For fixed $G,x,v$, $W_v$ is finite and nonnegative. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves (R). The earlier commentary about Klee faces can be reconstructed exactly. In the source family $G_m$, the minimal face at uniform marginals consists of three edge-disjoint matchings $M_1,M_2,M_3$, each of size $m$, partitioning the edges. A law on this face is uniquely $p\in\Delta_3$. At any point of its relative interior,

\[

\]

At $p=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$, the exact unrooted deficit is

\[

\]

\[
 \left(3-\frac{3m}{4}\right)\sum_i a_i^2.               \tag{Khess}
\]

Thus for **every $m>4$** it is a strict local maximum on the whole minimal face. The uniform law has edge covariance $2/9$ on same-colour coordinates and $-1/9$ on different colours. Its two positive eigenvalues are $m/3$, the remaining eigenvalues zero; at this point the unrooted separable Hessian is $-3I/4$. The normalized second-variation eigenvalues are therefore $1-m/4<0$. Constraints not tight at the uniform point have positive slack. In fact for $m>4$ this is a strict local maximum in the **full** polytope as well. \[

\]

The smooth function $J=F-3B/2$ is Lipschitz in a neighborhood of the uniform point, where all edge coordinates stay away from 0 and 1; $\|x'-y\|=O(r)$. Therefore

\[

## 3. Complete polynomial implementation of the stipulated prophet construction

### 3.1 A single submodular minimization returns the exact largest flat

Let E have n elements, M be a matroid, D a known subset, P a known flat, and kappa a positive integer. The source uses the largest flat Q containing P that maximizes

`f(Z)=|D intersect Z|-kappa r(Z)`.

On subsets A of `E\P`, define

`g(A)=(n+1)[kappa r(P union A)-|D intersect (P union A)|]-|P union A|`.  (SM)

This is an integer-valued submodular function: restriction of rank to supersets of P is submodular, and both cardinality terms are modular. A constant may be subtracted to normalize `g(empty)=0` before applying a normalized SFM interface.

The primary quantity in square brackets is integral. Changing it by at least one outweighs every possible change, of magnitude at most n, in the last cardinality term. Thus minimizing g first minimizes the primary quantity and then maximizes cardinality among its minimizers.

Every minimizer is closed. If `Z=P union A` is not closed, adjoining its missing closure elements does not increase rank, cannot increase the primary quantity, and strictly reduces the negative-cardinality term. This contradicts minimality. So minimizing over all subsets yields a flat primary minimizer, not a relaxation requiring a rounding step.

The primary minimizers over subsets containing P are closed under union and intersection, by submodularity and equality of their optimal values. Their union is the unique inclusionwise largest one and the unique maximum-cardinality one. Equivalently, source `lem:density` gives this fact on the flat lattice. Consequently the unique minimizer of (SM), after adjoining P, is **exactly the source's Q**. Arbitrary tie-breaking by an SFM implementation cannot change the rule.

A rank evaluation uses at most n independence queries by greedy scanning. All values in (SM) have O(log n+log kappa) bits. With the source's fixed `kappa=2^100`, SFM therefore has polynomial independence-query and bit cost. This is the critical computational step; no enumeration of flats is needed.

### 3.2 Finite path computation and rational arithmetic

Retain every source constant and coin law: `B=2^32`, `kappa=2^100`, and guard/eligibility probability `t=2^-140`. Draw the branch coin, all masks, and parity initially, exactly as prescribed. Dyadic membership probabilities use a bounded number of unbiased bits per label, so the full seed has O(n) bits. Nothing is concealed from the order adversary.

For a positive binary rational p/q, compute the rounded level `floor(log_B(p/q))` using numerator/denominator bit lengths and exact shifted-integer comparisons. The relevant shifts have magnitude bounded by a constant times the observation's bit length. Zero has its separate source branch. At most n levels are listed; gaps between their integer exponents do **not** generate auxiliary path steps.

Perform the source's candidate tests on the revealed labels. Sort the listed groups by their rounded level. For each listed group h and each integer auxiliary time in `[-3m-2,0]`, where `m<=n` is the number of listed groups, compute the nominal density expansion by (SM), then the guarded closure from the source equation `eq:paths`. Compute nominal entries at k+1 before the corresponding guarded entry. Values above zero are E and sufficiently low values are the loop flat by `lem:paths`. Thus O(n²) density calls suffice. Standard greedy rank/closure tests perform the other work. Storing all paths as subsets uses O(n³) bits.

At arrival, compute the candidate test from revealed H, check its listed group, inspect the stored nominal birth and final layer endpoints, and use the source's single conditional-rank test. The unknown full true groups and the optimal comparison set I* never need to be computed. The source's marked-pivot patterns and residual certificates are never enumerated by the algorithm.

Hence preprocessing and all n online decisions together take polynomially many independence queries and polynomial bit operations in n and the total length of the rational samples/values read. Preprocessing uses only samples; later values are read only when their labels arrive. Every path and decision agrees with the source for every seed and every permutation. The one-sample simulation therefore preserves the stated `2^-310` expected guarantee against every measurable full-seed order rule, and prefix feasibility holds deterministically.

This theorem concerns rational observations. It does not provide a Turing encoding or a uniform finite-precision guarantee for arbitrary exact real observations. Approximate rank or erroneous independence answers are also outside its scope.

### 3.3 Significance and adversarial checks

The O(n²) path bound comes directly from the source's activation schedule; the only additional operation is a classical modular perturbation followed by SFM. I therefore classify the result as technical only. A materially new target would need, for example, an improved selection mechanism or a justified reduction in the oracle cost beyond this generic implementation, not an additional corollary of the same simulation.

The diagnostic compares (SM) with exhaustive flat optimization on 2,688 binary representable matroid instances, including loops, parallel columns, multiple primary minimizers, and varied integer density charges. It also checks the residual-density inequality for every subset of each small ground set. These are finite implementation checks; the proof above applies to arbitrary oracle matroids, including nonrepresentable ones.

## 4. A sharp entropy estimate on subcubic graphs

### 4.1 Exact statement

Let G be any finite loopless multigraph on 2m>=2 vertices, with maximum degree at most three (parallel edges counted separately), and at least one perfect matching. For every x in P(G),

`F(x)-H(x) <= (1-1/m) c3 B(x)`,

`c3=log(3)/(2 log(3/2))`.  (SC)

For each m the coefficient is best possible among these graphs. For m>=2 it is best possible even among simple graphs. This is a proved technical deduction, not a general-degree theorem or a significance acceptance.

### 4.2 The scalar three-probability inequality

For `p1+p2+p3=1`, `pi>=0`, put

`h(p)=-sum pi log pi`, `b(p)=-sum (1-pi)log(1-pi)`.

Then `h(p)<=c3 b(p)`. Here and throughout, endpoint products are interpreted continuously. I give the proof so the crucial scalar step is not left as an estimate to assume.

Write c=c3 and `f(u)=-u log u+c(1-u)log(1-u)`. One has `1<c<2`, `f(0)=f(1)=0`, and

`f''(u)=-1/u+c/(1-u)`.

It is negative below `a=1/(c+1)` and positive above a. The continuous function `sum f(pi)` attains its maximum on the simplex. On its boundary, the two nonzero coordinates p,1-p give `(1-c)h(p,1-p)<=0`.

At an interior maximum, the derivatives f'(pi) agree. There cannot be two coordinates strictly greater than a: the second derivative in their difference direction would be positive. There cannot be two coordinates at least a with one strictly greater either. If two equal a, the third is `1-2a<a`, and strict decrease of f' on `(0,a)` contradicts stationarity. If all coordinates are at most a, strict decrease on that interval forces equality, giving p=(1/3,1/3,1/3), where `sum f(pi)=0` by the definition of c.

In the remaining case exactly one coordinate exceeds a. Neither other coordinate can equal a, since f' has its strict minimum there. Thus the other two lie below a and stationarity forces them equal. Write them t,t and the large coordinate 1-2t; then `0<t<1/3`. It suffices to check

`g(t)=2f(t)+f(1-2t)<=0` for `0<=t<=1/3`.

For `u=(1-2t)/t>=1`, direct differentiation gives

`g'(t)/2 = k(u):=log u-c log((u+1)/2)`.

Now `k(1)=0` and `k'(u)=[1-(c-1)u]/[u(u+1)]`. Since `1<c<2`, k increases to a single positive maximum and then decreases to minus infinity. It has exactly one further zero on `(1,infinity)`. As t increases, u decreases. Thus g first decreases and then increases on `(0,1/3)`; its maximum on this interval is at an endpoint. Both endpoint values are zero: g(0)=0 and g(1/3)=3f(1/3)=0. This proves the scalar inequality, including every boundary case.

### 4.3 Lift to matching entropy and prove sharpness

At a vertex v the chosen incident edge is a categorical variable with probabilities `(x_e:e incident to v)`. There are at most three categories; pad with zeroes and apply the scalar inequality. Summing over vertices counts each labelled edge twice, hence

`F(x)<=c3 B(x)`.  (L)

For **any** law p on perfect matchings of mean x, the star choice at each vertex is a function of the whole matching. Thus `Ent(p)>=h(x_delta(v))` at every vertex. Averaging these 2m inequalities yields

`Ent(p)>=F(x)/m`.

In particular `H(x)>=F(x)/m`. Combining with (L) proves

`F-H <=(1-1/m)F <=(1-1/m)c3 B`,

including m=1, zero coordinates, disconnected graphs, and value-one edges.

For sharpness use exactly the source's Klee graphs G_m and means `x_e=1/3` from `ex:prop-klee-face`. The source proves

`H=log3`, `F=m log3`, `B=2m log(3/2)`.

Both inequalities just used are equalities. The graphs are simple for m>=2 and subcubic at every m. At m=1, three parallel edges give H=F and B>0, so the zero coefficient is also optimal. No fresh extremal construction is being claimed.

### 4.4 Why this does not prove the general target

The improvement is exact but elementary after the source's extremizers: the matching law is only used through the entropy of a function. It should not be submitted as a nonroutine finding under the I07/I14/I15/I17 standard.

The scalar step already fails at degree four for coefficient 3/2. For a uniform four-category star, `h=log4` and `b=3log(4/3)`, with `h>(3/2)b`; equivalently `3^9>4^7`. This is not merely a probability vector with no graph realization. In the simple graph K6 minus a perfect matching, edge symmetry gives a feasible uniform mean x_e=1/4. There are eight perfect matchings, so its actual maximum entropy at this mean is log8, and this graph is **not** a counterexample to the target. It shows precisely that the scalar domination route cannot pass to general degree by the same proof.

Finite checks enumerate the source triangle expansions through m=7, retaining all perfect matchings and verifying that the recursively tight cuts leave exactly the three distinguished ones. The scalar inequality is also tested on all 16,471 ternary rational distributions with denominator 180. Floating-point entropy evaluations are diagnostics only; Sections 4.2–4.3 give the general proof.

## 5. Tight-cut decomposition: a complete identity and the unresolved term

### 5.1 Exact entropy gluing

Let G be a loopless labelled multigraph, x in P(G), and S a proper odd set with `x(C)=1`, `C=delta(S)`. Contract the two sides as in source `geom:lem-gluing`, obtaining G1,G2 and restricted means x1,x2. Write `q=(x_e:e in C)`, a probability vector, and `h(q)=-sum q_e log q_e`.

Then

`H_G(x)=H_G1(x1)+H_G2(x2)-h(q)`.  (G)

**Proof.** Every matching in a law of mean x crosses C an odd positive number of times. Expected crossing number one forces exactly one crossing almost surely. Let E_C be its crossing label and M1,M2 the two contracted matchings. They determine the original matching, and E_C is determined by each of them. The conditional entropy inequality gives

`Ent(M1,M2)<=Ent(M1)+Ent(M2)-h(q)`.

Their means are x1,x2, proving the upper bound in (G). Conversely take separate entropy-maximizing laws at x1,x2. Sample E_C with law q and, conditional on its value, sample those laws independently conditioned on that edge. Ignore q_e=0 labels. The **source's existing gluing construction** makes this a valid matching law with mean x, and conditional independence makes its entropy exactly the right side of (G). This proves equality. No compatibility of separate arbitrary completions is assumed: the shared crossing label is fixed before gluing. ∎

Define `D_G=F_G-H_G` and `b(q)=-sum (1-q_e)log(1-q_e)`. Crossing labels occur once in G and twice in the contracted pair, so

`D_G(x)=D_G1(x1)+D_G2(x2)`,

`B_G(x)=B_G1(x1)+B_G2(x2)-b(q)`.  (DB)

Therefore for `E_c=F-cB-H`,

`E_c(G,x)=E_c(G1,x1)+E_c(G2,x2)+c b(q)`.  (SEP)

This positive separator term is the obstruction to the proposed simple induction. Individual inequalities `E_c(Gi,xi)<=0` do not establish the parent inequality. Iterating any finite valid cut decomposition gives

`E_c(root)=sum_leaf E_c(leaf)+c sum_split b(q_split)`.

The missing step for c=3/2 is an **aggregate negative leaf allowance paying this entire separator sum**, or a different global entropy argument. No such estimate is proved here. It is not legitimate to drop the term, replace it by zero because the cut is tight, or assume the contracted means can be optimized independently while changing their crossing marginals.

In the source's Klee family, decomposition into K4 leaves has m-1 leaves and m-2 splits. Each split has q=(1/3,1/3,1/3). Formula (DB) recovers exactly `D=(m-1)log3` and `B=2m log(3/2)`. This is a useful adversarial check: already the source's coefficient-one failure is explained by cumulative separators. It also confirms why sharp face dimension alone cannot be substituted for a new entropy estimate.

The source trace obstruction, combined only with `d>=s-3m+2`, yields `0>=2+(c-2)m`. At c=3/2 this is consistent for m>=4; there is no contradiction. One needs information beyond that scalar trace and codimension pair. The subcubic argument supplies such information only in its restricted degree range.

### 5.2 A precise near-tight statement, with its computational limit

Let `S1,...,Sk` be any fixed finite family of odd sets, and put `delta_j=x(delta(Sj))-1>=0`. Let `beta=(sum delta_j)/2<1/2`. Choose an entropy-maximizing law p of mean x. Let Good mean that every specified cut is crossed once.

There is a feasible mean y on the intersection of those tight-cut faces such that

`||x-y||_infinity<=beta`,

`|H(x)-H(y)|<=h2(beta)+beta log N(G)`,  (NT)

where h2 is binary entropy with natural logarithms. The conditional law `p(.|Good)` realizes y and is entropy maximizing at y. No laminarity is needed for this statement.

**Proof.** If a matching crosses Sj more than once, it crosses at least three times. Markov's inequality applied to the nonnegative excess gives probability at most delta_j/2. A union bound gives `q=P(not Good)<=beta`, so Good has positive probability. Conditioning changes total variation by exactly q, hence changes each edge mean by at most q. Every specified cut then has mean crossing count one.

The conditional law maximizes entropy at its own mean y. Otherwise replace it by a higher-entropy law of mean y and retain the bad conditional law and mixture weight q. Any matching law of mean y crosses every selected cut once almost surely, so the replacement stays in Good. The original overall mean remains x and the mixture entropy increases, contradicting maximality of p.

Let Hg=H(y), and Hb be the entropy of the bad conditional law if q>0. Since Good is determined by the matching,

`H(x)=h2(q)+(1-q)Hg+q Hb`.

Both conditional entropies lie in `[0,log N(G)]`. Thus the absolute difference from Hg is at most `h2(q)+q log N(G)`, which is at most the right side of (NT), because q<=beta<1/2 and h2 increases there. The q=0 case is exact. ∎

This is a standard conditioning bound, not a new entropy algorithm. It depends on an entropy-maximizing input law, and its error grows with log N(G). The supplied FPRAS for a uniform law is not such a sampler at prescribed x. Even if such a sampler were available, rejection sampling would merely implement the conditioning with expected trials at most `1/(1-beta)`; it would not supply the missing separator allowance in (SEP). No dimension-free or relative-error improvement is asserted.

Exact rational diagnostics check the conditional product identity on 9, 45, and 225 crossing-one matchings of K6, K8 and K10, respectively. Separate positive Gibbs laws with dyadic crossing penalties verify the parity/slack bound, exact total variation after conditioning, and every coordinate perturbation bound. These computations support (G)/(NT), not the unresolved general coefficient.

## 6. An explicit obstruction to the global-bin correspondence transfer

In the list proof, different bins are automatically mutually nonconflicting because an actual color has one global bin. To copy this feature to a correspondence assignment, a bin map b on list entries must satisfy

`b(a)=b(a') for every forbidden pair aa'`.  (BIN)

Otherwise selecting entries in different bins could still create a forbidden pair, so stable sets within individual bins would not certify a coloring. Condition (BIN) forces b to be constant on each connected component of the cover graph (the graph with only forbidden-pair edges, as in the source's convention).

For every integer k>=2, take the base cycle `v0 v1 v2 v3 v0`, with `L(vi)={(vi,j):j in Z/kZ}`. On the first three edges match identical second coordinates; on the closing edge match `(v3,j)` to `(v0,j+1)`. These are legitimate perfect edgewise matchings. In the cover, a path of length four runs

`(v0,j)—(v1,j)—(v2,j)—(v3,j)—(v0,j+1)`.

Iterating j visits all 4k entries. The cover is a connected cycle, so every map satisfying (BIN) uses only one bin over the entire assignment. There is no way to give each list a positive fraction of many globally nonconflicting bins by this method.

This failure is not a coloring lower bound for large k. For k>=3 the choices `(0,1,0,1)` at the four vertices form a valid coloring. For k=2 the three identity edges force alternation and the closing shift forbids it, recovering the familiar even-cycle DP obstruction. Thus the bin problem persists even on an elementary colorable graph with arbitrarily large lists, not merely at an insufficient-list endpoint.

Two attempted repairs remain unproved:

* **List-local bins followed by conflict deletion.** Independent local partitions avoid forced global collapse, but leave forbidden pairs between differently named bins. The list proof's arbitrary eligible sets control vertex coverage, not the distribution of these surviving forbidden entry pairs. A bound preserving the linear color budget throughout the adaptive thinning stages is missing.
* **Apply the clique-free DP bound inside the minor recursion.** The source fixes clique order r and maximum degree Delta. Setting r=t from a K_t-minor exclusion does not give an absolute constant; a degeneracy bound does not give a maximum-degree bound for the entire graph. Stars already separate these degree notions. The partitioned adjustment lemma controls weighted local triangles but does not supply the minor-recursion palette reservation or an absolute-in-t quantitative estimate.

These are failures of two specific transfers. They do not show the linear DP statement false, or exclude a different use of the source's stronger local adjustment/independent-set-richness interfaces.

an important result, [25] proved such a bound for the hard-core distribution over matchings in a graph. This
led to resolving several questions involving asymptotic graph and hypergraph problems. For instance results

1.1 Our Contribution
We first show that good enough succinct representations exist for max-entropy distributions. Subsequently,
we give an algorithm that computes arbitrarily good approximations to max-entropy distributions given θ
and access to a suitable counting oracle for M . Our algorithm is efficient whenever the corresponding count-
ing oracle is efficient. Moreover, the counting oracle can be approximate and/or randomized. This allows
us to leverage a variety of algorithms developed for several #P-hard problems to give algorithms to compute
max-entropy distributions. Consequently, we obtain several new and old results about concrete algorithms to
compute max-entropy distributions. Interesting examples for which we can use pre-existing counting oracles
to obtain max-entropy distributions include spanning trees, matchings in general graphs, perfect matchings
in bipartite graphs (using the algorithm from [21]) and subtrees of a rooted tree. The consequence for perfect
matchings in bipartite graphs makes the algorithmic strategies for TSP/ATSP mentioned earlier computa-
tionally feasible, see Section 4. In the reverse direction we show that if one can solve, even approximately,

distribution. The goal in our problem is to find an γ that maximizes the entropy. In fact, given a γ , problem specific MCMC methods
can be used to generate a random sample from M according to the product distribution corresponding to γ .

oracles. This establishes an equivalence between counting and computing max-entropy distributions in a
general setting. As a corollary, we obtain that the problem of computing max-entropy distributions over per-
fect matchings in general graphs is equivalent to the, hitherto unrelated, problem of approximately counting
perfect matchings in a general graph.

1.1.1   Informal Statement of Our Results
Before we describe our results a bit more technically, we introduce some basic notation. For M ⊆ {0, 1}m ,
let P(M ) denote the convex hull of all M where each M ∈ M is thought of as a 0/1 vector of length m,
denoted 1M . Thus, given a θ , for the max-entropy program to have any solution, θ ∈ P(M ). Since we are
concerned with the case when M is given implicitly and may be of exponential size, we no longer hope to
solve the max-entropy convex program directly since that may require exponentially many variables, one for
each M ∈ M . Thus, we work with the dual to the max-entropy convex program. The dual has m variables
and, if θ is in the relative interior of P(M ), the optimal dual solution can be used to describe the optimal
solution to the max-entropy convex program, which is a product distribution. In fact, we assume one can
put a ball of radius η around θ and it still remains in the interior of P(M ). Importantly, our algorithm
requires access to a generalized counting oracle for M , which given γ can compute ∑M∈M , M∋e ∏e′ ∈M γe′
for all e ∈ [m] and also the sum ∑M∈M ∏e∈M γe . We also consider the case when the oracle is approximate
(possibly randomized) and for a given ε , can output the sums above up to a multiplicative error of 1 ± ε .
The following is the first main result of the paper, stated informally here.

Theorem 1.1 (Counting Implies Optimization, See Theorems 2.6 and 2.8) There is an algorithm which,
given access to a generalized (approximate) counting oracle for M ⊆ {0, 1}m , a θ which is promised to
be in the η -interior of P(M ) and an ε > 0, outputs a γ such that its corresponding product probability
distribution p is such that H(p) ≥ (1 − ε/η )H(p⋆ ) and for every e ∈ [m],

the oracle is bounded by a polynomial in the input size, ln 1/η and ln 1/ε .

A useful setting for η and ε to keep in mind is 1/m2 and 1/m3 respectively. The bit-lengths of the inputs to the
counting oracle are polynomial in 1/η and, hence, the running time of our algorithm depends polynomially
on 1/η . If the generalized counting oracle is ε -approximate, the same guarantee holds. Note that for many
approximate counting oracles, the dependence on ε on their running time is a polynomial in 1/ε . Hence, in
this case the running time depends polynomially on 1/ε . Finally, note that this result can be easily gener-
alized to obtain algorithms for the problem of finding the distribution that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler
divergence from a given product distribution subject to the marginal constraints, see Remark 2.12.

algorithm to the dual of the max-entropy convex program. While it is more convenient to work with the
